prompt: A learner explains that heating a reaction mixture by 10 °C roughly doubles the rate "because the molecules move faster, so they collide more often". Evaluate this explanation.
answer: The mechanism named is real but far too small to account for the effect. The dominant cause is the fraction of collisions that exceed the activation energy.
explanation: Both effects occur, and their sizes are very different. Average molecular speed goes as √T, so heating from 293 K to 303 K raises the collision FREQUENCY by only about 1.7% — nowhere near a doubling. What changes dramatically is the shape of the tail of the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution: the proportion of molecules with kinetic energy above the activation energy rises exponentially with temperature, and for a typical Ea that 10 °C is enough to roughly double it. So the extra collisions contribute a couple of per cent and the extra SUCCESSFUL collisions contribute essentially all of the rest. The learner has named a genuine contribution and mistaken it for the main one, and the test that separates them is quantitative rather than conceptual.

prompt: A learner reasons that since increasing the concentration of a reactant speeds up a reaction, doubling the concentration of the limiting reactant must also double the mass of product obtained. Evaluate the learner's reasoning.
answer: Two separate claims are bundled together. The rate claim is right; the yield claim is right only by coincidence of wording, and the reasoning given for it is wrong.
explanation: Rate and yield are set by different things. Rate depends on how often particles collide with enough energy, so a more concentrated solution has more particles per unit volume, more collisions per second, and a faster reaction — that part is sound. The amount of product, by contrast, is fixed by stoichiometry: how many MOLES of the limiting reactant are present, and in what ratio the equation consumes them. Doubling the concentration of the limiting reactant in a fixed volume does double the moles present, so the yield does double — but for a reason the learner never states, and their reasoning would give the same answer in cases where it is false. Doubling the concentration of a reactant in EXCESS speeds the reaction up and changes the yield not at all. So the inference "faster, therefore more" fails, and separating it from "more moles, therefore more" is the point.

prompt: A learner states that an exothermic reaction needs no activation energy, "because it releases energy rather than absorbing it". Evaluate this claim.
answer: The claim is wrong, and if it were right, petrol could not be stored safely.
explanation: Activation energy and heat of reaction are different quantities read off different parts of an energy diagram. Ea is the height of the barrier between reactants and products, and it must be climbed before any reaction can occur, because existing bonds have to be stretched and broken before new ones form and release energy. ΔH is the difference in level BETWEEN reactants and products, and for an exothermic reaction it is negative — the products end lower than the reactants. A reaction can be strongly exothermic and still have a high barrier, which is exactly the case for the combustion of petrol: ΔH is large and negative, and yet a tank of it sits unreacted in air indefinitely until a spark supplies the activation energy. The learner's picture predicts that every exothermic reaction should start spontaneously, which would make fuels, explosives and food impossible to store.

prompt: A learner claims that a catalyst can only work if it is in the same phase as the reactants, "because it has to mix with them in order to take part". Evaluate this claim.
answer: The claim is wrong. Heterogeneous catalysis, in which the catalyst is a different phase, is the basis of most industrial chemistry.
explanation: A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants and does behave roughly as the learner pictures — it enters the mechanism, forms an intermediate, and is regenerated. A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase, typically a solid working on gases or a solution, and it works at its SURFACE: reactant molecules adsorb onto active sites, which holds them in the right orientation and weakens their bonds, lowering the activation energy; the products then desorb and free the site. Nothing needs to dissolve. This is how the iron catalyst in the Haber process, the vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process and the platinum-rhodium in a car's catalytic converter all operate, and it is industrially preferred precisely because a solid is easy to separate from the products. The learner's requirement would rule out most of the catalysis actually in use.

prompt: A learner claims that at a high enough temperature every collision between reactant particles will result in a reaction, "because they will all have more than the activation energy". Evaluate this claim.
answer: The claim is wrong on both counts: the distribution of energies has no upper cut-off, and energy alone does not guarantee a reaction.
explanation: The Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution always has a spread, at every temperature. Raising the temperature shifts and flattens it so that a much larger FRACTION of molecules exceed Ea, but the curve still stretches down toward zero energy, so there are always slow molecules and always collisions too gentle to react. The fraction approaches one only as an unreachable limit. The second omission matters just as much: a successful collision needs correct ORIENTATION as well as sufficient energy. Molecules that meet with ample energy but the wrong parts facing each other simply bounce apart, which is why rate equations carry a steric factor alongside the exponential energy term, and why reactions between large, awkwardly shaped molecules are slow even when heated hard.

prompt: A learner describes a catalyst as lowering the activation energy and "therefore making the reaction more exothermic, since more energy is released overall". Evaluate this description.
answer: The first half is correct and the second does not follow. A catalyst leaves ΔH completely unchanged.
explanation: On an energy diagram a catalyst lowers the peak by offering an alternative pathway, but it does not move either end: the reactants start at the same level and the products finish at the same level, so ΔH, the difference between them, is identical with or without it. The learner has read the lowered barrier as energy released, when it is energy that no longer has to be supplied and then recovered on the way down. The barrier is also lowered by the same amount in BOTH directions, so the reverse reaction is accelerated equally — which is why a catalyst cannot shift the position of an equilibrium. If a catalyst did change ΔH, it would be possible to release net energy by running a reaction forward with a catalyst and back without one, repeating indefinitely, which is a perpetual motion machine and violates conservation of energy.

prompt: A plant supervisor budgets for regular catalyst replacement, explaining that "the catalyst is slowly used up in the reaction, so it has to be topped up". Evaluate the supervisor's explanation.
answer: The budget is justified and the explanation is not. A catalyst is regenerated by the reaction; what depletes it in practice is poisoning and physical degradation.
explanation: A catalyst takes part in the mechanism and is released again unchanged, so it appears on neither side of the overall equation and, in principle, one portion could run the reaction forever. That is what distinguishes a catalyst from a reactant. Real industrial catalysts nevertheless do need replacing, for reasons outside the stoichiometry. Impurities in the feedstock — sulfur compounds are the classic case — bind irreversibly to the active sites and block them, which is catalyst poisoning, and is why cars with catalytic converters must use unleaded petrol. Heat gradually sinters a finely divided solid catalyst into larger particles with less surface area, and solid deposits such as carbon can bury the surface. The supervisor's spending is sound; the reason given would predict a replacement rate proportional to output, and the real one is driven by feed purity and operating temperature.

prompt: A learner advises that an industrial reaction should always be run at the highest temperature the plant can manage, "because a higher temperature always gives more product". Evaluate this advice.
answer: The advice is wrong as a general rule. Higher temperature always gives product FASTER, and for an exothermic equilibrium it gives LESS of it.
explanation: Rate and yield must be separated. Raising the temperature always increases the rate, because more collisions exceed the activation energy — so the reaction reaches its end point sooner, and for a reaction that goes essentially to completion the learner's advice does no harm to the yield. For a reversible reaction it does. By Le Chatelier's principle, raising the temperature shifts an equilibrium in the ENDOTHERMIC direction, so for an exothermic forward reaction the equilibrium yield falls as the plant runs hotter. The Haber process is the standard illustration: ammonia synthesis is exothermic, so a low temperature would favour the yield, and at low temperature the reaction is far too slow to be useful. Industry settles on a compromise of about 450 °C with an iron catalyst — fast enough to be economic, cool enough to leave a workable yield.

prompt: A learner grinds a lump of marble to powder before reacting it with hydrochloric acid, and reports that the finer powder "gave more carbon dioxide, which proves that surface area increases the yield". Evaluate the learner's conclusion.
answer: The conclusion is wrong. Surface area changes the rate, not the yield — the powder most likely finished, and the lump had not.
explanation: Grinding exposes far more of the solid to the acid, so more particles are available to collide at any moment and the reaction runs faster. The total amount of CO₂ obtainable is fixed by the moles of the limiting reactant and the stoichiometry of CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂, and grinding changes neither. What the learner has almost certainly measured is the gas collected within a fixed time, by which point the powder had reacted completely and the lump had not. Two checks settle it: leave both until fizzing stops and collect the same volume from each, or plot volume against time and note that the two curves rise at different rates to the SAME plateau. Treating a rate measurement as a yield measurement is the error, and a stopwatch that runs long enough removes it.
